title: Ibn al-Haytham and the Science of Light
summary: How the medieval scholar Ibn al-Haytham used dark-room experiments to study light and vision, and why he is called an early experimental scientist.
poll: Testing an idea yourself is better than trusting what a famous book says.

versions.title: The Man Who Studied Light
versions.text:
How do we see? Long ago, a man asked this. His name was Ibn al-Haytham. He was a scholar. He was born in Basra. That was more than a thousand years ago. Then he lived in Cairo.

Old books said our eyes send out rays. He did not just trust the books. He wanted to test it.

He said light comes from the sun or a lamp. It hits things. Then it goes to our eyes. That is how we see. He showed one more thing. Light goes in straight lines.

He did a fun test. He sat in a dark room. The room had one small hole. Light came in. A street scene showed on the wall. It was an image. But it was upside down!

He set lamps by the hole. Each lamp made its own spot of light. He hid one lamp. Its spot was gone.

He liked to observe and test. He wrote down what he saw. He wrote a big book on light. Lots of folks read it.

So, many call him an early scientist. He did an experiment to find what was true.

In his time, some old books said that our eyes send out rays. He did not just trust the books. He wanted to test the idea.

He showed that light comes from the sun, a lamp, or a fire. It bounces off things. Then it goes into our eyes. That is how we see. He also showed that light moves in straight lines.

One test used a dark room. There was a tiny hole in one wall. Light came in through the hole. An image of the scene outside showed up on the far wall. But it was upside down!

He liked to observe and test. He wrote down what he saw. He wrote a big book about light. Later, people in Europe read it, too.

Now, many call him an early scientist. He did not just guess. He did an experiment to check each idea.

versions.title: Ibn al-Haytham and the Science of Light
versions.text:
How do we see the world around us? More than a thousand years ago, a curious thinker set out to answer this question. His name was Ibn al-Haytham. He was born around the year 965 in Basra, in what is now Iraq. Later, he lived and worked in Cairo, Egypt. He studied mathematics, astronomy, and especially light.

In his time, many people relied on a theory from ancient Greek writers. It said that our eyes send out rays. The rays touch objects, and that lets us see them. Ibn al-Haytham respected these writers, but he did not simply accept their ideas. He wanted evidence.

After careful study, he decided that light comes from a source, such as the sun or a lamp. It bounces off objects and travels into our eyes. He also showed that light moves in straight lines.

One of his most famous experiments used a dark room with a tiny hole in one wall. Light from outside passed through the hole. It formed an image of the scene on the far wall. To his surprise, the image was upside down. Today, this kind of room is called a camera obscura, Latin for "dark room."

He also placed several lamps outside the hole. Each lamp made its own spot of light inside the room. When he covered one lamp, only its spot disappeared. This helped prove that light travels in straight lines.

He wrote down his method and results in a large work called the Book of Optics. Later, it was translated into Latin, and scholars in Europe studied it for centuries.

Today, many historians describe Ibn al-Haytham as one of the first experimental scientists. He tested ideas instead of just accepting them. He based each conclusion on what he saw.

versions.title: Ibn al-Haytham and the Science of Light
versions.text:
More than a thousand years ago, an inquisitive thinker set out to answer a deceptively simple question: how do human beings actually perceive the world around them? His name was Ibn al-Haytham, subsequently known throughout Europe as Alhazen. He was born around the year 965 in Basra, in present-day Iraq, eventually living and working in Cairo, Egypt, where he investigated mathematics, astronomy, and, above all else, the behavior of light. His contributions to the discipline now called optics were so substantial and far-reaching that he is frequently regarded as one of its principal founders.

During his lifetime, numerous scholars relied upon a theory inherited from ancient Greek writers, according to which the eyes emit rays that travel outward to reach objects, thereby allowing people to perceive them. Ibn al-Haytham respected these earlier philosophers considerably. He categorically refused to accept their conclusions without rigorous, independent examination, arguing forcefully that a genuine seeker of truth ought to scrutinize everything he reads rather than trust any established authority blindly, regardless of that authority's reputation.

After an extended period of meticulous investigation, he concluded that light originates from a luminous source, such as the sun or a lamp, reflects off the surfaces of surrounding objects, and subsequently travels into the eye, where vision actually occurs. He also conclusively demonstrated that light propagates in uniformly straight lines. Furthermore, he analyzed refraction in considerable detail, the systematic bending of light as it passes from one transparent material, such as air, into a different one, such as water or glass.

One of his most celebrated experiments employed a darkened chamber with a tiny aperture cut into one wall. Light entering from outside passed through this aperture and projected an image of the external scene onto the opposite wall, and remarkably, the resulting image appeared entirely inverted. Today, this arrangement is called a camera obscura, Latin for "dark room," and it is widely regarded as an early conceptual ancestor of the modern photographic camera.

He also positioned several separate lamps outside the aperture at the same time, and each individual lamp produced its own distinct spot of illumination inside the chamber. When he deliberately concealed one particular lamp, only its corresponding spot of light vanished from the wall, while the others remained entirely unaffected. This carefully controlled evidence strongly supported his central hypothesis that light travels in straight, unbending lines rather than curving or spreading unpredictably.

Ibn al-Haytham meticulously documented his experimental methodology and his conclusions in a substantial work titled the Book of Optics, which was translated into Latin many centuries later and subsequently studied extensively by European scholars for generation after generation. In 2015, designated the International Year of Light and organized in cooperation with UNESCO, the world celebrated approximately a thousand years since he first composed this influential treatise.

Today, many historians consistently describe Ibn al-Haytham as one of the very first experimental scientists in recorded history. He tested his ideas systematically through careful, repeatable experimentation rather than simply accepting inherited wisdom, and he based every one of his conclusions firmly on careful, documented observation rather than speculation alone.

versions.title: Ibn al-Haytham and the Science of Light
versions.text:
More than a thousand years ago, an inquisitive thinker set out to answer a deceptively simple question: how do human beings actually perceive the world around them? His name was Ibn al-Haytham, subsequently known throughout Europe as Alhazen, and he was born around the year 965 in Basra, in present-day Iraq, eventually living and working for much of his career in Cairo, Egypt, where he investigated mathematics, astronomy, and, above all else, the physical behavior of light itself. His contributions to the discipline now called optics were so substantial and far-reaching across subsequent centuries that he is frequently regarded by historians of science as one of its principal founders.

During his lifetime, numerous scholars relied upon a theory inherited directly from ancient Greek writers, according to which the eyes emit rays that travel outward through space to reach objects, thereby allowing people to perceive them visually. Ibn al-Haytham respected these earlier philosophers considerably, acknowledging their contributions to learning, but he categorically refused to accept their conclusions without rigorous, independent examination of his own, arguing forcefully and repeatedly that a genuine seeker of truth ought to scrutinize everything he reads rather than trust any established authority blindly, regardless of that authority's considerable historical reputation.

After an extended period of meticulous investigation conducted over many years, he concluded with confidence that light originates from a luminous source, such as the sun or a lamp, reflects off the surfaces of surrounding objects, and subsequently travels into the eye itself, where the actual process of vision occurs. He also conclusively demonstrated, through careful experimentation, that light propagates in uniformly straight lines rather than curving unpredictably, and furthermore, he analyzed refraction in considerable mathematical detail, the systematic bending of light as it passes from one transparent material, such as air, into a different one, such as water or glass, a phenomenon with important implications for lenses.

One of his most celebrated experiments employed a darkened chamber with a single tiny aperture deliberately cut into one wall. Light entering from the brightly lit world outside passed through this narrow aperture and projected a complete image of the external scene onto the opposite interior wall, and remarkably, the resulting image appeared entirely inverted, upside down relative to the scene it depicted. Today, this ingenious arrangement is called a camera obscura, Latin for "dark room," and it is widely regarded by historians of technology as an early conceptual ancestor of the modern photographic camera.

He also positioned several separate lamps outside the aperture simultaneously, and each individual lamp produced its own distinct, separate spot of illumination inside the darkened chamber. When he deliberately concealed any one particular lamp from view, only its corresponding spot of light vanished from the interior wall, while the remaining spots stayed entirely unaffected by the change. This carefully controlled, systematic evidence strongly supported his central hypothesis that light invariably travels in straight, unbending lines rather than curving, scattering, or spreading unpredictably through the intervening space.

Ibn al-Haytham meticulously documented his experimental methodology and his resulting conclusions in a substantial scholarly work titled the Book of Optics, a text that was translated into Latin many centuries after its original composition and subsequently studied extensively by generations of European scholars who built upon its foundations. In 2015, designated internationally as the International Year of Light and organized in cooperation with UNESCO, the world formally celebrated approximately a thousand years since he first composed this remarkably influential treatise on the nature of light.

Today, many historians of science consistently describe Ibn al-Haytham as one of the very first true experimental scientists in recorded human history, because he tested his ideas systematically through careful, repeatable experimentation rather than simply accepting inherited wisdom at face value, and because he based every one of his conclusions firmly on careful, documented observation rather than on speculation or received authority alone.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Ibn al-Haytham invented the first modern camera in Cairo.
Ibn al-Haytham used experiments to learn how light and vision work.
Ancient Greek writers proved that our eyes send out rays.
The Book of Optics was first written in Latin for Europeans.
questions.why: The article explains how Ibn al-Haytham tested ideas about light and vision with experiments and recorded what he found.

wrong.A: The camera obscura is a dark room, not a modern camera.
wrong.C: The Greek writers had a theory, and Ibn al-Haytham questioned it.
wrong.D: The book was translated into Latin later; it was not first written in Latin.

questions.stem: According to the article, what did the older theory say?
options: Light travels only in curved paths.
Images in dark rooms appear upright.
Light comes from the sun into the eye.
The eyes send out rays that reach objects.
questions.why: The article says the theory from ancient Greek writers claimed that the eyes send out rays that reach objects.

wrong.A: The article says nothing about curved paths in the old theory.
wrong.B: Images in the dark room appeared upside down.
wrong.C: This was Ibn al-Haytham's own conclusion, not the older theory.

questions.stem: What happened to the Book of Optics later?
options: It was lost and never found again.
It was rewritten as a book of poems.
Scholars in Europe studied it in Latin.
It was kept secret by scholars in Basra.
questions.why: The article says the book was translated into Latin and studied by European scholars for centuries.

wrong.A: The book was translated and studied, so it was not lost.
wrong.B: The article does not mention poems.
wrong.D: The article says it was shared widely, not kept secret.

questions.stem: In the article, the word evidence means—
options: facts or signs that show something is true
a story that people tell for fun
a guess that no one can check
a rule that everyone must follow
questions.why: He wanted evidence instead of simply accepting ideas, and his lamp test gave facts showing that light travels in straight lines.

wrong.B: Evidence is not a story told for fun.
wrong.C: A guess that cannot be checked is the opposite of evidence.

questions.stem: Why did a lamp's spot disappear when he covered that lamp?
options: The room became too warm for the light.
Its light could no longer reach the hole.
The other lamps blocked all of its light.
The image on the wall turned upside down.
questions.why: Each spot was made by light traveling straight from one lamp through the hole, so blocking the lamp removed its spot.

wrong.A: The article does not mention heat.
wrong.C: The other lamps made their own spots; they did not block light.
wrong.D: The image was already upside down; that did not make the spot disappear.

questions.stem: If a famous book made a claim about light, what would Ibn al-Haytham most likely do?
options: Accept it because the writer was famous
Ignore it and never read the book again
Copy it into his own book without change
Design a test to see if the claim was true
questions.why: The article shows that he respected older writers but wanted evidence, so he would test the claim.

wrong.A: He did not accept ideas just because they came from respected writers.
wrong.B: He read and respected older books; he did not ignore them.
wrong.C: He based his conclusions on what he observed, not on copying.

questions.stem: Why did Ibn al-Haytham most likely need the room to be dark?
options: So the faint image would be easy to see
So the lamps outside would burn slowly
So no one could watch his secret work
So the room would stay cool in summer
questions.why: The image made by the small hole is dim, so it shows clearly only when no other light fills the room.

wrong.B: Darkness inside would not change how the lamps outside burn.
wrong.C: The article gives no sign that his work was secret.
wrong.D: The article does not connect the dark room to temperature.

questions.stem: How does the author organize most of the article?
options: By comparing Basra and Cairo in detail
By listing steps for building a camera
By describing an old idea, then his tests and results
By telling a made-up story about a lamp
questions.why: The article first explains the older theory, then describes his experiments, then tells what came of his work.

wrong.A: The cities are only mentioned briefly.
wrong.B: The article does not give building steps.
wrong.D: The article is nonfiction, not a made-up story.

MID.prompt: Explain how the dark-room experiments helped Ibn al-Haytham learn about light. Use at least two details from the article.
checklist: I described at least one of his experiments.
I explained what the experiment showed, using details from the article.
I used words like first, then, and because to connect my ideas.
MID.modelAnswer: The dark-room experiments helped Ibn al-Haytham learn about light by giving him real evidence instead of just an old theory. First, he let light pass through a tiny hole into a darkened room, and he observed that it formed an upside-down image of the scene outside on the opposite wall. Then, he placed several lamps outside the hole, and when he covered one lamp, only its matching spot of light disappeared inside the room. Because of this careful method, he reached the conclusion that light travels in straight lines, and his results were later translated into Latin for scholars in Europe to study.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Ibn al-Haytham advanced optics by testing ideas through experiments.
Ibn al-Haytham proved that every Greek idea about science was wrong.
The camera obscura was invented in Europe after the Latin translation.
Refraction is the most important discovery in the history of optics.
questions.why: The article focuses on how his experiments and systematic observation changed the understanding of light and vision.

wrong.B: He questioned one Greek theory of vision; the article does not say every Greek idea was wrong.
wrong.C: The article describes his own dark-room experiments, not a European invention.
wrong.D: Refraction is one topic he studied, not the main idea.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is refraction?
options: The reflection of light off a mirror
The way the eyes send out rays
The bending of light between materials
The image formed in a dark chamber
questions.why: The article defines refraction as the bending of light as it passes from one material, such as air, into another, such as water or glass.

wrong.A: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface, not bending.
wrong.B: This was the older theory of vision.

questions.stem: By what name did Ibn al-Haytham become known in Europe?

Euclid
Avicenna
Alhazen

wrong.B: Euclid was an ancient Greek mathematician, a different person.
wrong.C: Avicenna is the European name of a different scholar, Ibn Sina.

questions.stem: He argued that a seeker of truth should not "trust any authority blindly." What does authority mean here?
options: a small opening in a chamber wall
an expert or source that people trust
a lamp used during an experiment
a translation of an older book
questions.why: In context, authority refers to respected writers, like the Greek thinkers, whose ideas people accepted as expert knowledge.

wrong.A: A small opening is the aperture, not an authority.
wrong.C: Lamps were tools in his experiment.
wrong.D: A translation is a version of a book in another language.

questions.stem: What conclusion did the lamp experiment support?
options: Light bends when it enters water.
The eyes emit rays toward objects.
Light travels in straight lines.
Images in dark rooms are upright.
questions.why: Because covering one lamp removed only its spot, the experiment supported his hypothesis that light travels in straight lines.

wrong.A: Refraction is discussed separately, not in the lamp experiment.
wrong.B: His work challenged this older theory.
wrong.D: The dark-room image appeared upside down.

questions.stem: Why does his belief that people should not "trust any authority blindly" matter for science?
options: Scientists must check claims with evidence.
Scientists should never read old books.
Scientists must always agree with experts.
Scientists should work only in dark rooms.
questions.why: Science depends on testing claims rather than accepting them because of who made them, which is exactly what he did.

wrong.B: He respected and read older works; he simply tested their ideas.
wrong.C: This is the opposite of his belief.
wrong.D: Dark rooms were one tool, not a rule for all science.

questions.stem: Why was the Latin translation of the Book of Optics likely important?
options: It made the book shorter and easier to sell.
It let European scholars learn from his work.
It proved the book was first written in Europe.
It replaced his name with a Greek scholar's.
questions.why: Latin was read by scholars in Europe, so the translation let them study his ideas for generations.

wrong.A: The article says nothing about shortening or selling the book.
wrong.C: He wrote it in the Islamic world; it was translated later.
wrong.D: He became known as Alhazen, not by a Greek scholar's name.

questions.stem: Why does the author open the article with a question about how people see?
options: To argue that vision can never be explained
To list the different parts of the human eye
To compare the cities of Basra and Cairo
To introduce the problem he worked to solve
questions.why: The opening question leads into the problem Ibn al-Haytham investigated: how light and vision work.

wrong.A: The article shows that he did explain much about vision.
wrong.B: The article does not list the parts of the eye.
wrong.C: The cities are mentioned only as places where he lived.

HIGH.prompt: Many historians call Ibn al-Haytham one of the first experimental scientists. Do you agree that he deserves this title? Support your position with evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence supports my position.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that Ibn al-Haytham deserves to be called one of the first experimental scientists, because he refused to accept the authority of earlier Greek theories on faith and instead tested his own hypothesis through careful experimentation. Rather than assuming that the eye simply sent out rays, he built a darkened room and systematically observed that light entering through a hole formed an upside-down image, which supported his idea that light travels from a source in straight lines. He strengthened this evidence by arranging multiple lamps outside the hole and showing that covering one lamp removed only its matching spot of light inside. Because he recorded his systematic methods and conclusions in the Book of Optics, a work that shaped the study of optics for centuries, I think the title of experimental scientist truly fits him.
